mechanism.attack: The proposed chain (acoustic wave generation → enhanced fluid mixing → improved heat transfer coefficient → reduced thermal gradients) presupposes that acoustic streaming and cavitation meaningfully augment convective transport in a packed battery module geometry. The cited correlation Nu = C·(f·ρ·P/μ)^0.5·Pr^0.33 is presented as if it were a validated closed-form, but no constants C are given, no Reynolds-like acoustic regime is specified (Stuart number, Euler number), and the exponent of 0.5 on the (f·ρ·P/μ) group is not derivable from first principles for oscillatory flow in narrow, parallel-plate battery cooling channels where the acoustic wavelength at 20–100 kHz (λ ≈ 1.7–8.6 cm in air at 20 °C) is comparable to or larger than typical channel gaps (2–10 mm). In that regime the flow is quasi-steady incompressible oscillation, dominated by velocity boundary layers at the plate walls, not by streaming-driven bulk mixing. Cavitation in dielectric coolants requires tensile pressures on the order of the vapor pressure (~kPa to ~MPa depending on fluid), which at the stated frequencies demands acoustic intensities far above what 4-cell bench transducers can deliver without arcing near cell terminals. The mechanism collapses in real channel geometry.
mechanism.basis: At 20–100 kHz in air λ ≈ 3.4–17 mm, and in typical dielectric liquids λ is roughly an order of magnitude larger; channel gaps of 2–10 mm place the geometry in the incompressible-oscillation regime where streaming-induced mixing is confined to thin boundary layers, so bulk convective enhancement predicted by the stated 0.5-power correlation does not materialize.

boundary_conditions.attack: The candidate states "effective at 20–100 kHz" and "limited in high-viscosity fluids" but provides no upper bound on fluid viscosity, no minimum acoustic intensity to overcome threshold streaming onset, and no cavitation threshold (peak negative pressure vs. vapor pressure). Worse, the boundary condition omits the dominant constraint: battery modules contain flammable organic electrolyte vapors. Acoustic cavitation at these frequencies in the presence of flammable gas mixtures is a documented ignition source. The candidate does not bound acoustic pressure amplitude below the minimum ignition energy threshold for the electrolyte decomposition products (typically ethylene, methane, hydrogen at elevated cell temperatures). Also unaddressed: transducer insertion in a sealed, vibration-sensitive cell stack introduces mechanical fatigue on cell housings; IEC 62660 and UN 38.3 vibration testing would have to be re-qualified, an undisclosed constraint.
boundary_conditions.basis: Acoustic cavitation in flammable organic vapors generated by Li-ion electrolyte at elevated SoC and temperature is a known ignition-initiation mechanism; no stated bound on peak negative acoustic pressure exists in the candidate, leaving a credible fire/explosion failure path.

equations.attack: Nu = C·(f·ρ·P/μ)^0.5·Pr^0.33 is dimensionally inconsistent. The group (f·ρ·P/μ) has dimensions of [Hz·(kg/m³)·W/(Pa·s)] = [s⁻¹·kg·m⁻³·kg·m²·s⁻³·m·s·kg⁻¹] = m⁻³·s⁻³. Taking a 0.5 power gives m⁻¹·⁵·s⁻¹·⁵, which is not dimensionless and cannot form a Nusselt number when multiplied by C·Pr^0.33. There is no published correlation of this exact form for acoustic-enhanced convection in channel flow; the form resembles a forced-convection correlation but with f substituted for a velocity scale, which is invalid because frequency alone does not characterize oscillatory transport — the relevant scale is the acoustic velocity amplitude, not frequency. The equation is fabricated.
equations.basis: Dimensional analysis of the right-hand side: (f·ρ·P/μ)^0.5·Pr^0.33 yields units of m⁻¹·⁵·s⁻¹·⁵ ≠ dimensionless, so Nu cannot equal this expression. The correlation is dimensionally invalid.

evidence.attack: The single cited record is doi:10.5281/zenodo.19488056 ("sonic tech"). Zenodo deposit identifiers of the form 10.5281/zenodo.19488056 are user-uploaded, minimally-reviewed repositories (Zenodo's policy is no peer review), and the descriptor "sonic tech" gives no title, author, journal, year, or experimental data. A single unrefereed repository record tagged generically does not constitute evidence supporting the specific claim that acoustic streaming reduces Li-ion cell temperature rise by 30–50%. No measured Nu, no measured ΔT, no measured acoustic intensity, no cell chemistry specified. This is not evidence; it is a placeholder.
evidence.basis: The only cited record (doi:10.5281/zenodo.19488056) is a Zenodo upload with the vague label "sonic tech"; Zenodo does not perform peer review, the record provides no quantitative data on Nu, ΔT, or acoustic power, and a single such deposit cannot substantiate a 30–50% performance claim.

prior_art.attack: The retrieved record doi:10.1016/j.ultsonch.2025.107570 ("A review on ultrasound-enhanced heat transfer") is marked MECHANISM and teaches the underlying phenomenon — ultrasound-enhanced heat transfer — including acoustic streaming and cavitation mechanisms. Combined with doi:10.1007/s10973-023-12100-9 (heat-pipe battery thermal management review), the mechanism class is not unexploited. Furthermore, the candidate's intervention — embedding transducers in cooling channels — is a generic instantiation of ultrasound-assisted heat exchange that the Ultrasonics Sonochemistry review explicitly surveys across multiple heat-exchanger geometries. The "unexploited phenomenon" claim is contradicted by an existing comprehensive review covering the same physics.
prior_art.basis: doi:10.1016/j.ultsonch.2025.107570 is a review on ultrasound-enhanced heat transfer that directly covers acoustic streaming and cavitation for heat transfer augmentation, pre-empting the "unexploited phenomenon" assertion.

predicted_effect.attack: A predicted 30–50% reduction in battery pack temperature rise during fast charging is implausible given the dominant thermal resistance in Li-ion packs. During fast charge at ~2–4C, heat generation is dominated by Joule heating in the cell core (I²R_cell), not by external convective resistance. The Biot number for a prismatic/pouch cell during fast charging is typically Bi ≈ 0.1–0.5 (core-to-surface), meaning the internal conduction resistance is comparable to or larger than the external convective resistance. Enhancing external h by 30–50% via acoustic streaming reduces total thermal resistance by at most ~10–20% (since 1/(1/U_new) calculation: if R_conv = R_int, halving R_conv reduces R_total by 25%; if R_conv is only 30% of R_total, the same enhancement reduces ΔT by ~9%). The stated 30–50% ΔT reduction requires that convective resistance dominate, which contradicts standard Li-ion thermal models (see for example the heat-pipe review doi:10.1007/s10973-023-12100-9 which characterizes these resistances).
predicted_effect.basis: For Li-ion cells during fast charge with Bi ≈ 0.1–0.5, internal conduction resistance is comparable to or larger than external convective resistance; doubling external h (a 100% enhancement) reduces total thermal resistance by at most 25%, so a realistic acoustic enhancement of 30–50% in h yields ΔT reduction of ~9–17%, not 30–50%.

experiment_design.attack: The "killer experiment" specifies a 4-cell bench rig with acoustic transducers and temperature sensors. The kill condition is "no temperature reduction observed at acoustic power levels below cell damage threshold." This kill condition is unfalsifiable in practice because (1) "acoustic power levels below cell damage threshold" is a wide-open range — any negative result can be attributed to running below an unspecified optimal intensity, and (2) the experiment does not control for transducer parasitic heating, which is substantial at the stated frequencies (piezoelectric transducers at 20–100 kHz dissipate 10–30% of input electrical power as heat, directly warming the coolant). Without a calorimetric control (a duplicate rig with electrically driven but acoustically inactive dummy transducers of identical dissipation), a measured ΔT could be positive due to transducer self-heating, not negative due to the mechanism — and the experiment cannot distinguish these. The design cannot kill the mechanism because it can always be blamed on insufficient intensity, and positive results are confounded by transducer heat.
experiment_design.basis: Piezoelectric transducers at 20–100 kHz typically dissipate 10–30% of input electrical power as heat, confounding any temperature measurement; without a matched dummy-transducer control, the experiment cannot isolate acoustic-streaming effects from transducer self-heating, and the kill condition allows indefinite escalation of acoustic power to avoid falsification.

buyer.attack: The buyer persona "EV battery pack thermal engineers" would not adopt this technology because (1) automotive qualification (UN 38.3, IEC 62660-2/3, USABC abuse testing) requires years of reliability data that bench acoustic rigs cannot supply, (2) adding piezo transducers per cell module adds cost, mass, EMI/EMC noise sources (ultrasonic drivers generate conducted and radiated emissions in the 20–100 kHz band and harmonics, problematic for CAN/LIN bus and BMS ADC front-ends), and (3) no automotive OEM has a deployed acoustic-cooling battery pack on a production EV program. The buyer cannot purchase what cannot be qualified, and the candidate provides no path to qualification. Furthermore, the MECHANISM prior-art (ultrasound-enhanced heat transfer review) is well-known to thermal engineers, who have already evaluated and not adopted acoustic cooling for the same reasons.
buyer.basis: Automotive battery qualification under UN 38.3, IEC 62660-2, and USABC abuse protocols requires multi-year reliability testing that a bench 4-cell rig cannot substitute; no production EV currently uses acoustic-enhanced battery cooling, indicating the buyer class has already screened this approach and rejected it.
